wiki-iran.standing: Wikipedia pageviews for the article on Iran, a daily count of how many people look the country up. Attention series like this rise when a place enters a crisis and decay as the story settles, so the shape tracks public alarm more than events themselves.
wiki-iran.recent: The decline follows the shift from open war to bargaining over the Strait of Hormuz: Trump halted the attack on Iran's infrastructure on 2 August, and by 4 August talks with Oman and the US to reopen the strait were reported making progress. Fighting continues at the margins — US Hellfire missiles crippled a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman — but Iran has reopened its damaged airports.

brent.standing: The price of a barrel of North Sea crude, and the benchmark most of the world's oil is priced against. It moves on supply — a strike, a sanction, a strait — and fuel, freight and fertiliser move after it.
brent.recent: Hormuz is the whole story. Two ADNOC tankers were struck transiting the strait on 13 August, and Trump's claim that the US controls it followed a halted attack on Iran and stalled talks. War-risk premiums, not barrels, are doing the work: Pakistan lifted diesel to 383.95 rupees a litre. Drone strikes hit Novorossiysk and Libya's Zawiya refinery.

wti.standing: The price of a barrel of US light sweet crude, the benchmark American oil is priced against and the reference for US refiners and drillers. It moves on supply, policy and demand, and fuel and freight costs move after it.
wti.recent: Attacks on oil infrastructure kept a war premium in the price: two ADNOC tankers were struck transiting Hormuz, a third drone strike hit Libya's Zawiya refinery, and a Ukrainian drone attack on Nizhnekamsk killed 13 deep inside Russia. US diesel reached $5.36 a gallon. The barrel is still well below its May high.

natgas-hh.standing: The US benchmark price for natural gas, set at a Louisiana pipeline hub and used to price most American gas contracts. It sets what power plants, factories and heating bills pay, and it moves on weather, storage and how much gas is being shipped out as LNG.
natgas-hh.recent: The series has drifted down about 9% over the window, from $3.34 on May 29 to a low of $2.56 on Aug 7, without a clear cause in view. Demand-side commitments kept building: SpaceX said it would build its own natural gas power plants for a Texas chip factory, and Amazon backed a Fort Stockton plant of 35 turbines.

wheat.standing: The world reference price for milling wheat, quoted per tonne. It is the input cost behind bread, flour and animal feed, so a move in it lands on household food bills — hardest in countries that import most of what they eat.
wheat.recent: Russia set ablaze Ukraine's largest Danube grain port at Izmail, while drought across Europe dried soils through a record-hot summer. The FAO price index reached 131.1, and in Karachi a 20kg flour bag now costs Rs3,000 after a wheat import tender delay.

rice.standing: The world price of a tonne of milled rice, the staple grain for roughly half the planet. It is set by a thin export market — a handful of countries sell most of it — so an export ban or a bad monsoon in one of them lands on import bills everywhere.
rice.recent: Rice has moved the other way from the rest of the food basket: the series is down 29% to $400 a tonne, well below its Aug 2024 high of $563.8 and near the Oct 2025 low of $330.6. That falls against the Food and Agriculture Organization's index hitting 131.1, a three-year high driven by heatwaves and wars pushing up crop costs.

copper.standing: The price of a tonne of refined copper, the metal that carries current in every grid, motor and building wire. Demand tracks electrification and construction, and supply sits with a handful of mines, so the price reads as a gauge of how fast the world is wiring itself.

us-10y.standing: The yield on ten-year US government debt, the benchmark price of borrowing for the world's largest borrower. It sets the floor under mortgages, corporate credit and sovereign spreads everywhere, and moves on inflation, Fed policy and demand for Treasuries.
us-10y.recent: The yield sat near the top of its range after the BOJ held rates at 1% on 31 July while warning underlying inflation was running above its 2% target, the same day the series peaked at 4.75%. Since then the dollar fell to its weakest since May as a rate hike came into doubt, and Trump again moved to fire Cook, reviving the fight over Fed independence.

sp500.standing: A capitalisation-weighted index of 500 large US-listed companies, and the standard benchmark for American equities. Most US retirement money tracks it, so its level is the number against which pensions, funds and corporate valuations are measured.
sp500.recent: The index climbed to its 61-day high on Aug 13, up roughly 5 percent from its Jun 10 low. Little in the record explains the run directly: the visible corporate news was Tata Group stocks falling with TCS down nearly 4 percent, Tesla's denial of a report on selling its China business, and McDonald's delaying store expansion plans. Oil eased and stocks gained on Hormuz reopening hopes on Aug 4.

nasdaq100.standing: A stock index tracking the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq exchange, weighted by market value. Chipmakers, cloud providers and consumer platforms dominate it, so it moves as a proxy for the technology trade.
nasdaq100.recent: The index sits near the top of its 61-day range after recovering from a Jul 29 low. The stories driving the sector are capital ones: Nvidia arranged $500 billion in financing through six lenders to fund purchases of its own chips, Amazon is funding a Texas gas plant next to a datacentre, and DRAM prices jumped from $39 to $145.

us-gas-retail.standing: The average price American drivers pay at the pump, tracked weekly across the country. It follows crude oil with a lag of a week or two, and because almost every household buys it, it feeds into inflation expectations faster than any other consumer price.
us-gas-retail.recent: Refineries have been the target rather than the crude itself: Ukrainian drones hit two Russian refineries on 6 August and reached Nizhnekamsk on 10 August, 1,600 km from the border, while a third drone strike burned Libya's Zawiya refinery on 11 August. Retail has still eased from the May 18 high of $4.49 to $4.01.

natgas-ttf.standing: The European benchmark price for natural gas, set at the Dutch TTF hub and the reference for most gas traded across the continent. It is what heating, electricity generation and fertiliser and chemical production are priced off, and industry contracts follow it.
natgas-ttf.recent: The price sits well above its December low, and the pipeline politics behind European supply stayed live: Russia's envoy accused Germany of seeking a scapegoat over the Nord Stream attack and predicted only formal measures in response. Demand-side pressure is building elsewhere too, with SpaceX planning natural gas power plants for a Texas chip factory.

vix.standing: A CBOE index of expected S&P 500 swings over the coming month, derived from options prices. It is the market's price of insurance against a fall, so it rises when equity investors pay up for protection.
vix.recent: Volatility has drained out of markets across the window, with the index at its lowest reading of the period on Aug 12 after peaking at 22.22 on Jun 10. The same calm shows up elsewhere: bitcoin volatility nearly vanished as ETFs took in $754 million, and traders read the sell-off from $65,000 as thin volume rather than panic.

fx-pkr.standing: The exchange rate of Pakistan's rupee against the US dollar. Pakistan imports its fuel, edible oil and much of its industrial input in dollars, so the rate sets the domestic price of energy and food and the size of the country's import bill.
fx-pkr.recent: The rupee has held in a narrow band near 277.8 while the import bill did the moving: Ogra's fortnightly revision put high-speed diesel at 383.95 rupees a litre, with war-risk premiums in Hormuz feeding into landed crude costs. Islamabad has asked Washington for a $10 billion dollar line to shore up reserves.

fx-ngn.standing: The exchange rate between Nigeria's naira and the US dollar. Nigeria earns most of its foreign currency from crude oil exports, so the rate tracks oil receipts and central-bank reserves, and it sets the cost of nearly everything the country imports.
fx-ngn.recent: The naira held in a narrow band, easing about 1.2% over the month from its Jul 22 high of 1381 to 1363. Abuja approved deep offshore tax incentives pitched at unlocking $50 billion in oil investment, and the Senate opened audit hearings that Seplat Energy skipped — but neither moved the rate far, and the input does not explain the drift.

fx-egp.standing: The exchange rate of Egypt's currency against the dollar. Egypt imports most of its wheat, fuel and medicine, so the rate sets the domestic price of staples and the cost of servicing the state's foreign debt.
fx-egp.recent: The pound has firmed from its late-July low, but the earlier devaluation is still working through Cairo's shelves: a drug pricing freeze set against import costs has left pharmacies empty, and the government is weighing flexible pricing in response. Egypt's feud with Ethiopia and its absence from the Mecca defence pact frame the same constraint.

fx-try.standing: The exchange rate of Turkey's currency against the dollar, quoted as lira per dollar so a rising number means a weaker lira. It is the price at which a large emerging economy imports its energy and services its foreign-currency debt.
fx-try.recent: The lira drifted to a fresh 30-day low as Ankara reshaped its security position: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Mecca joint defence pact on 7 August and Ankara's defence ministry said standing political and military mechanisms would follow, while parliament passed a Kurdish disarmament law and Turkey rationed Bosphorus passage for vessels bound for Novorossiysk.

fx-bdt.standing: Bangladesh's currency against the US dollar. It prices the country's garment export earnings and its imports of fuel, food and cotton, and it sets the local cost of the remittances that millions of families abroad send home.
fx-bdt.recent: The taka held a narrow band through the window, easing from 124 on Aug 7 to 122.7 on Aug 14 — a move of well under half a percent. The month's politics ran hotter than the currency: Dhaka pressed Delhi over ex-prime minister Hasina's planned virtual address, which India denied any involvement in.

fx-idr.standing: Indonesia's currency, quoted as rupiah per US dollar, so a higher number means a weaker rupiah. Southeast Asia's largest economy prices its commodity exports and dollar debt against it, and Bank Indonesia defends it.
fx-idr.recent: The rupiah firmed to 17,840 after Prabowo nominated a Bank Indonesia deputy as the central bank's new governor on 11 August, a continuity pick that settled the main open question for the currency. It has recovered from 18,110 on 28 July, touching 17,800 on 8 August.

fx-lbp.standing: The Lebanese pound's exchange rate against the US dollar. Long fixed by the central bank, it collapsed during Lebanon's banking crisis and now trades at a rate that sets the price of nearly everything in a country that imports most of what it consumes.
fx-lbp.recent: The pound has barely moved, holding near the top of its 30-day range after peaking on Aug 7. The pressure on Lebanon is physical rather than monetary: Israeli strikes and demolitions across the south, a seventh round of direct talks in Rome, and 4,333 killed in the south since March by the Lebanese count.

fx-cny.standing: The exchange rate of China's currency against the US dollar, quoted as yuan per dollar so a lower number means a stronger yuan. Beijing manages it within a daily band, making it a policy signal as much as a price, and it sets the cost of Chinese goods worldwide.
fx-cny.recent: The yuan drifted to the strong end of its 30-day range, reaching 6.744 on Aug 14 from 6.775 on Jul 18 — a move of about a third of a percent, well inside normal daily variation. Nothing in the month's China news, from Beijing's tightened drone export controls to the US accusation that China is evading tariffs, explains a move that small.

fx-inr.standing: The exchange rate between India's currency and the US dollar. It sets the local price of India's imported crude, fertiliser and electronics, and it moves on oil, US interest rates and foreign flows into Indian markets.
fx-inr.recent: The rupee has firmed roughly 1% over the month, from 96.65 on 18 July to 95.05 on 5 August, tracking the 4.5% fall in oil after a remark on Iran — India buys its crude in dollars, so cheaper barrels shrink the import bill. It has since eased back to 95.43 as July retail inflation rose to 4.45% from 4.38%, with onion prices up 22.54%.

fx-brl.standing: The exchange rate of Brazil's currency against the US dollar, quoted as reais per dollar, so a rising number means a weaker real. It is the price at which the region's largest economy imports, borrows and sells its iron ore, soy and oil.
fx-brl.recent: The real has drifted weaker across the month, with the softest reading on 14 August. Washington revoked the visa of Brazil's ambassador on 4 August, tying its restoration to Brasília accepting its own choice of envoy, and the Workers' Party nominated Lula da Silva for a fourth presidential term on 2 August.

fx-mxn.standing: The exchange rate of Mexico's peso against the US dollar, one of the most heavily traded emerging-market currencies. Mexico sends most of its exports to the United States, so the rate carries trade policy, remittances and cross-border investment.
fx-mxn.recent: The peso strengthened to its 30-day high after Mexico and Peru restored diplomatic relations, ending an asylum row. Domestic security news dominated the period: the US offered $25 million for a CJNG leader, and an alleged betrayal split the Sinaloa Cartel in two. None of it explains the currency's drift directly.

fx-eur.standing: The exchange rate between the euro and the US dollar, quoted here as euros per dollar. It is the world's most heavily traded currency pair, and the rate sets the import price of energy and commodities — sold in dollars — for the whole euro area.

fx-jpy.standing: The exchange rate between Japan's currency and the US dollar, quoted as yen per dollar, so a higher number means a weaker yen. It is the funding leg of the global carry trade and it sets the price of everything Japan exports and every barrel it imports.
fx-jpy.recent: Tokyo sold dollars for yen hours before the Bank of Japan held rates at 1% on 31 July, and the US joined the intervention on 3 August, pushing the dollar to a one-month low — the yen's strongest point of the window at 156.5. It has drifted back toward 159.4 since. Toyota's quarterly profit of $9.4 billion showed who benefits from the weaker side of the trade.

fx-rub.standing: The exchange rate of Russia's currency against the dollar, and the cleanest daily read on how sanctions, oil receipts and war spending are landing on the Russian economy. It sets the price of every import Russia still buys.
fx-rub.recent: The ruble weakened through a month of deepening strikes on Russian soil: a drone attack on Nizhnekamsk killed 13 some 1,600 km from the Ukrainian border, Ukraine hit the Novorossiysk naval base and port, and nearly $2 billion in Wildberries stock burned in depots. Moscow also ruled out a Ukraine freeze on Aug 9.

fx-zar.standing: The exchange rate of South Africa's currency against the US dollar, quoted as rand per dollar so a higher number means a weaker rand. It is one of the most heavily traded emerging-market currencies and moves with commodity prices, global risk appetite and domestic politics.
fx-zar.recent: The rand strengthened from 16.83 on Jul 25 to 16.15 by Aug 8, its firmest of the period, before easing to 16.19. Nothing in the material accounts for the move; domestic news over the window ran to governance stories — the Prasa security-contract case in Pretoria, undelivered vet clinic buses, and municipal electricity bills rising up to 14%.

btc.standing: The price of one bitcoin, the largest cryptocurrency and the one most held by funds, treasuries and exchange-traded products. It is priced against the dollar around the clock, and the rest of the crypto market tends to move with it.
btc.recent: A run of security failures set the tone: a Coldcard hack drained $120 million and congested the mempool with the attacker's own transactions, then attackers drained Foundation's and Citadel21's Lightning nodes. Bitcoin fell 4% against every other market signal and lagged a stock rally, sitting 49% below its record even as ETFs took in $754 million.

eth.standing: The second-largest cryptocurrency by value, and the settlement layer for most stablecoins, tokenized assets and decentralised trading. Its price moves with risk appetite across crypto, and with demand for the blockspace those applications consume.
eth.recent: Ether drifted through a narrow band, ending near $1,885 after a low of $1,841 on Jul 18 and a high of $1,952 on Jul 27. Regulation set the tone: Treasury sanctioned an Iranian dollar-token exchange, Brazil imposed a 24-hour delay on $10,000-plus transfers, and the Senate's Clarity Act missed its pre-recess vote window.

paxg.standing: A claim on a fixed weight of gold, priced per troy ounce and issued as a token backed by bars in a vault. It tracks the metal that central banks hold as reserves and that savers buy when they doubt currencies or the institutions behind them.
paxg.recent: Gold ran to a ten-week high, with spot hitting $4,392 an ounce Wednesday as markets braced for US inflation data — the series peaked at $4,404 on Aug 13. The metal's institutional demand also drew attention that day, when KPMG completed Tether's first full audit by physically counting the gold bars behind the stablecoin's reserves.

wiki-artificial-intelligence.standing: A measure of how many people open Wikipedia's overview article on artificial intelligence each day — a rough gauge of how far the subject has spread beyond the people who work on it, rather than of anything the technology itself is doing.
wiki-artificial-intelligence.recent: Readership climbed alongside a run of concrete disputes rather than one launch: invisible text in a Hartford legal filing that told AI models to side with the plaintiff, a company selling 'human-written' medical research that was itself AI, and Google's AI telling users a sunset had already happened. Seoul put $880 billion behind chips and power in the same window.

wiki-russia.standing: The Wikipedia article on Russia, and the daily count of people who open it. Attention to a country page runs on the news cycle rather than on the country, so it rises with wars, elections and disasters and falls back within days.
wiki-russia.recent: Readership climbed through the second week of August as Ukrainian drones reached far into Russia: a strike on Nizhnekamsk, 1,600 km from the border, killed 13 including a child, and Novorossiysk's naval base and port were hit on 12 August. Putin then threatened cargo-ship seizures from a warship off Sakhalin.

wiki-pakistan.standing: Daily readership of the English Wikipedia article on Pakistan — a country of some 250 million people, a nuclear-armed army, and a chronically fragile external account. Attention to it usually tracks war, elections or the economy rather than anything domestic.
wiki-pakistan.recent: Pakistan signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Mecca with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, and Ankara says the three will now build standing political and military mechanisms plus defence-industry cooperation. Days earlier, a suicide attack on a protest in Swat district killed 14 at a peace rally.

wiki-china.standing: Wikipedia's article on China, and a daily count of how many people open it. Attention to a country page tends to follow the days that country makes news, so the series works as a rough public-curiosity gauge rather than a measure of anything happening inside the country.
wiki-china.recent: Zhu Rongji, the premier who restructured China's state-owned enterprises and steered its WTO accession, died on 12 August at 97 — reforms under which tens of millions lost jobs. Typhoon Dolphin drove the earlier rise: China evacuated over a million people and closed major ports a day before landfall.

wiki-strait-of-hormuz.standing: The 21-mile-wide sea lane between Iran and Oman that every tanker leaving the Gulf must pass through. Roughly a fifth of the world's oil and a third of seaborne LNG moves through it, so its risk premium lands on import bills far away.
wiki-strait-of-hormuz.recent: Readership tracked the closure fight rather than the strait itself. Iran has kept Hormuz shut behind six conditions and a reparations demand, transits fell by a third, and Trump claimed "We own it" as the deal window narrowed. Two ADNOC tankers were struck transiting on 13 August.

wiki-bitcoin.standing: A count of how many people open the Bitcoin article on Wikipedia each day — a rough gauge of public curiosity about the asset rather than its price. Attention tends to arrive with the events that make holding it feel risky.
wiki-bitcoin.recent: The month's stories were about custody failing rather than price. A Coldcard hack drained $120 million and one firmware bug at a Toronto wallet maker let thieves take $88 million; attackers separately drained Foundation's and Citadel21's Lightning nodes, and an audit turned up 4,962 findings in a day. Bitcoin sits 49% below its record.

wiki-saudi-arabia.standing: A daily count of how many people read the English Wikipedia article on Saudi Arabia — a rough gauge of when the kingdom enters the global conversation, and of which events send outsiders looking for background on it.
wiki-saudi-arabia.recent: The 23 July peak preceded the run-up to the Mecca defence pact, signed 7 August by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan and read abroad as a 'Sunni NATO'. Readership held up through the Houthi strike that wounded 11 civilians in Najran and the Marib missile attacks, then eased as attention turned to the Strait of Hormuz talks.

wiki-donald-trump.standing: The Wikipedia article on the sitting US president, and one of the most-read biographies on the site. Its daily readership rises and falls with whatever the presidency is doing, making it a rough gauge of how much of the world's attention Washington is holding.
wiki-donald-trump.recent: Readership through early August tracked the Strait of Hormuz standoff — Trump halted attacks on Iran's infrastructure, then claimed the US fully controls the strait while Iran, Oman and US officials moved closer to a deal. Attention bottomed on Aug 1 and revived around the Ankara decoy flight, when Trump left hidden inside a catering truck.

wiki-india.standing: The Wikipedia article on India, the world's most populous country and its largest democracy. Daily readership rises when the country is in the news — elections, budgets, cricket, border incidents — and it is a rough proxy for global curiosity about India.
wiki-india.recent: Readership was flat across the month, holding near 29,570 views a day. The 6 August peak coincided with Modi inaugurating the Param Pragya AI supercomputer at Sonipat and with New Delhi geoblocking Bitchat's GitHub code during a shutdown; a US Senate bill threatening 100% tariffs on India was in the same week.

wiki-israel.standing: Wikipedia's article on Israel, and the number of people who open it each day. Readership climbs when the country is at the centre of a story, so the curve is a rough gauge of how far a Middle East event has travelled beyond the region.
wiki-israel.recent: The peak on Aug 11 came as Ramallah reported more than 500 attacks in the West Bank in a week and Caracas ended 17 years of severed ties with Israel. Around it: Israel's demolitions in south Lebanon, Netanyahu's rejection of the Gaza roadmap before the October 27 election, and soldiers emptying the besieged village of Qusra.

wiki-ukraine.standing: A daily count of how many people open the English Wikipedia article on Ukraine — a rough gauge of how far public attention to the war extends beyond the people already following it, and how quickly it fades between shocks.
wiki-ukraine.recent: Readership peaked on 22 July and has drifted down since, even as the war widened: Ukrainian drones killed 13 at Nizhnekamsk on 10 August, 1,600 km from the border, and hit Novorossiysk naval base on 12 August, while Russia burned the Danube grain port at Izmail and struck a Kyiv children's hospital.

wiki-nigeria.standing: A daily count of how many people open the English Wikipedia article on Nigeria — Africa's most populous country and its largest oil producer. It is a rough gauge of when a country pulls in readers who were not already following it.
wiki-nigeria.recent: Attention fell back from the late-July peak toward a story about money and the state: a currency dealer moved 785 million naira to coup plotters, and the EFCC's freeze on Osun's accounts was vacated on Tinubu's orders. The August news turned domestic — aviation unions struck in Lagos, and the Senate summoned oil firms over a skipped audit hearing.

cp:hormuz.standing: One-fifth of global seaborne oil passes through this 21-mile strait between Iran and Oman.
cp:hormuz.recent: Iran keeps the strait closed and has set six conditions for reopening, adding a reparations clause as the deal window narrows; 8 to 15 ships now cross daily. Two ADNOC tankers were struck transiting Hormuz on 13 August, and US Hellfire missiles crippled a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman. Diesel in Pakistan now costs 383.95 rupees a litre.

cp:bab-el-mandeb.standing: Between Yemen and Djibouti — the Red Sea’s southern gate. Houthi attacks since 2023 have pushed container shipping to reroute around Africa.
cp:bab-el-mandeb.recent: Traffic fell as Houthi missiles and drones widened past shipping to the coasts around it: a strike on Mokha, a claimed hit on the Jazan refinery, and a Bab al-Mandeb strike that killed six sailors. Escort requests are up 39% since February. Maersk, routing around the Cape, raised profit guidance to $6.5 billion.

cp:suez.standing: Egypt’s 120-mile artery carries roughly 12% of global trade. The 2021 closure disrupted supply chains for weeks; Red Sea instability keeps it volatile.

cp:malacca.standing: Between Malaysia and Sumatra — the fastest route between the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Over 80,000 ships a year, including most of China’s oil imports.
cp:malacca.recent: Traffic has run close to its 90-day baseline, near the top of a range whose low came on 19 July. The Hormuz closure has cut Gulf crude arriving in Malaysia and Hormuz vessel transits have fallen to a fraction, redirecting rather than reducing what moves through the strait.

cp:taiwan.standing: Between mainland China and Taiwan — roughly 40% of the world’s container traffic passes through, and the flashpoint of any US–China confrontation.
cp:taiwan.recent: Traffic sits about 15% below its 90-day baseline, and the collapse to 28 vessels on 10 July preceded the 401-vessel rebound two days later — a spike-after-halt pattern typical of weather backlogs rather than closure. Chinese coast guard ships have since patrolled east of Taiwan, off Orchid Island, and Typhoon Dolphin forced flight cancellations and evacuations in China on 9 August.

cp:panama.standing: 50-mile shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific. Drought in 2023–24 cut daily transits by half — a live example of climate binding to trade.
cp:panama.recent: Transits have run about 5% under their own 90-day baseline, with the window swinging from 83 vessels on Jul 13 to 22 on Jul 22 and 29 now. The input does not explain the swing; the drought reporting in this window covers Europe and the Danube, not the isthmus.

cp:bosporus.standing: Istanbul’s 20-mile waterway links the Black Sea to the Mediterranean — the only route for Russian naval access and Ukrainian grain exports.
cp:bosporus.recent: Turkey began rationing passage, turning back some vessels bound for Novorossiysk, as a drone campaign spread across the Black Sea: drones struck the Turkish-operated cargo ship Nadezhda near Novorossiysk on 4 August, one killed a crewman on a coal-hauling tanker, and Ukraine hit the Novorossiysk naval base on 12 August. Grain and crude traffic carries the cost.

cp:gibraltar.standing: 8 miles between Morocco and Spain — the only Atlantic–Mediterranean link. A surveillance chokepoint for Russian submarines and sanctioned oil.
cp:gibraltar.recent: Traffic sits near its own 90-day baseline, with the count down from a 13 June high of 163 vessels a day. The coverage names no closure or weather event here; wave heights stayed under a metre, and the disruption in the strait's news — the Ceuta crossings, where 72,000 people rushed a city of 84,000 — was a land border, not a shipping one.

cp:dover.standing: The busiest shipping lane on Earth — 400+ ships a day squeeze through the English Channel’s 21-mile narrows.
cp:dover.recent: Traffic drifted lower across the window, from 210 vessels a day on May 23 to a low of 126 on Aug 3, and sits near 168 now — a couple of percent under its own 90-day baseline with calm seas and no weather alert. The stories on this water have been the migrant crossings rather than the freight: 157 people on one dinghy off Boulogne-sur-Mer when its engine caught fire.

cp:cape-of-good-hope.standing: The 3,000-mile detour around southern Africa — the alternative when the Red Sea is closed. The new default for tankers since Houthi attacks began.
cp:cape-of-good-hope.recent: Traffic has fallen by about a fifth from its May 16 peak of 150 vessels a day, settling near 83 with rough seas and waves to 3m on the route. The pressure that pushed ships this way persists further north: a tanker reported two explosions near Hormuz on 6 August, Iran's Guard claimed two tankers disabled, and a sanctioned tanker off Oman is leaking a 400 square kilometre slick.

cp:kerch.standing: Between Crimea and Russia — the only access to the Sea of Azov. A flashpoint since 2014 and contested throughout the Russia–Ukraine war.
cp:kerch.recent: Traffic has gone to zero as strikes have made the northern Black Sea uninsurable for merchant shipping: war-risk premiums now price ships out of calling at Odessa, Russia burned Ukraine's largest Danube grain port at Izmail, and Ukrainian drones hit the Novorossiysk naval base. Putin has also threatened to seize cargo ships.

mkt:tadawul.standing: The Arab world’s largest exchange by market value, dominated by Aramco. Trades Sunday to Thursday, so it opens the global week before Tokyo.
mkt:tadawul.recent: The index sits below its mid-June level after weeks of Houthi fire reaching Saudi soil: strikes wounded 11 civilians in Najran, a claimed attack on the Jazan refinery that processes 400,000 barrels of crude daily, and a fire Aramco says was extinguished at its Jizan facility. Riyadh signed the Mecca defence pact with Turkiye and Pakistan on 7 August but has not retaliated.

mkt:bist.standing: Türkiye’s only exchange. Priced in lira, so its index level carries the country’s inflation as much as its earnings — read the direction, not the number.
mkt:bist.recent: The index has drifted lower over the window while Ankara reshaped its security position: Turkey signed a collective-defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in Mecca on 7 August, and passed a law on Kurdish disarmament on 10 August. Shipping risk sits closer to home — drones struck a Turkish-operated ship near Novorossiysk, and Turkey began rationing Bosphorus passage.

mkt:dfm.standing: The Gulf’s main listing venue for property and banking. Moved from a Sunday–Thursday week to Monday–Friday in 2022, unlike Riyadh.
mkt:dfm.recent: Two ADNOC tankers were struck transiting Hormuz on 13 August, and Iran made new demands around the strait days earlier; seven blasts hit Jebel Ali port on 5 August. The index sits well below its 18 June high of 6270, with 137,000 Gulf tourism jobs forecast lost.

mkt:bursa-malaysia.standing: The world’s largest market for Islamic finance instruments, and the centre of the global sukuk trade.
mkt:bursa-malaysia.recent: The index has drifted lower since peaking at 1748 on Aug 5, the day before Gulf crude exports to Malaysia dipped on the Hormuz closure. Vessel transits through the strait have fallen to a fraction of normal, and the squeeze has since reached Malaysian refineries.

mkt:idx.standing: The exchange of the world’s largest Muslim-majority country, heavily weighted to commodities and banking.
mkt:idx.recent: The index sits well below its May 18 high of 6,599 after a June 8 trough of 5,342, down about 4% over the window. On August 11 Prabowo nominated a Bank Indonesia deputy as the central bank's new governor, and the rupiah rose slightly on the news; the index has since been close to flat.

mkt:tse.standing: Asia’s largest exchange, and the first major market to price each trading day.
mkt:tse.recent: The index has climbed roughly a tenth over the window on a weak yen and the profits it delivers: Toyota's quarterly profit nearly doubled to $9.4 billion on the cheap yen, and the Bank of Japan held rates at 1% on 31 July. Currency policy has cut the other way, with a joint US-Japan intervention on 3 August pushing the dollar to a one-month low.

mkt:hkex.standing: Where mainland Chinese companies meet foreign capital — the clearest daily read on sentiment toward China.
mkt:hkex.recent: The index has drifted down over the quarter, from its May high to a June low and back to a level still well below where it started. The coverage points to friction rather than a single shock: Washington has accused Beijing of evading tariffs, Beijing has tightened drone exports, and Typhoon Dolphin forced port closures and the evacuation of over a million people. None of it explains the move on its own.

mkt:sse.standing: Mainland China’s main board. Largely closed to foreign investors, so it tracks domestic policy more than global risk appetite.
mkt:sse.recent: The index sits well below its May high, drifting through a stretch dominated by trade friction rather than domestic growth news: Beijing tightened drone exports as another US-China trade clash brewed, and Washington accused China of evading tariffs. Typhoon Dolphin closed major ports and cancelled flights in the same window.

mkt:krx.standing: Dominated by Samsung and SK Hynix — a proxy for the global semiconductor cycle.
mkt:krx.recent: The index is a memory trade: it fell hard through late July, then posted its largest single-day gain ever on 31 July, surging a record 18% to reclaim 6,500 on a chip rally after its steepest three-day rout. SK Hynix then dropped 5% on a $38bn fab commitment, with all 2027 memory capacity already sold out and Seoul staking $880bn on AI.

mkt:bse.standing: Asia’s oldest exchange, founded 1875, and the benchmark for Indian equities.
mkt:bse.recent: The index climbed to 78,950 on Aug 6 before easing, with domestic policy and corporate news dominating: parliament passed a mineral tax bill stripping states of mining royalty powers, and Tata Sons faced a leadership question as Chandrasekaran weighed quitting before an August 18 vote. July onion prices rose 22.54%, keeping imported inflation in view.

mkt:sgx.standing: Southeast Asia’s financial hub, weighted to banks and regional property.

mkt:twse.standing: TSMC alone is roughly a third of the index, which makes this the most concentrated major market on the map.
mkt:twse.recent: The index is up 11% over the quarter, with the low on 30 July falling within days of two Chinese coast guard ships drifting off Orchid Island, east of Taiwan, and the run to 45,940 has since resumed. Taipei says AI agents extracted passwords over four days in a hacking campaign, and Arizona has been pitching 100 Taiwanese investors on tax breaks to build beyond chips.

mkt:set.standing: Thailand’s benchmark, sensitive to tourism flows and regional energy prices.
mkt:set.recent: The index sits near the top of its 47-day range after climbing from May, with the day's fall coming amid a run of unsettled domestic news: the Nonthaburi school shooting that killed eight and prompted the Thai PM to promise stricter gun laws, Bangkok's reception of Min Aung Hlaing, and a crackdown on USDT transactions tied to scam compounds.

mkt:pse.standing: A small, domestically-driven market where remittance flows move the index.
mkt:pse.recent: The index sits near the top of its range after climbing off a late-May low, but slipped on the day. Manila's politics have run through the period: the Sara Duterte impeachment trial reached Day 14 with confidential-fund disbursements logged to unusual names and zero results, and a magnitude 6.3 earthquake struck the southern Philippines on 5 August.

mkt:asx.standing: Mining and banking. Often the first major market to react to Chinese demand data.
mkt:asx.recent: The index sits near its 6 August high of 9,272 after a 5% climb across the window. The RBA held rates steady on 11 August as the housing market softened, leaving another hike possible, and China's steel stock has aged into recycling — a scrap transition that skips Australian iron ore, the export the index's largest miners depend on.

mkt:jse.standing: Africa’s largest exchange by far, and the continent’s only one with a usable public daily series.
mkt:jse.recent: The index has drifted down from its Aug 7 high, retracing much of the climb off its Jul 23 low. The domestic backdrop is a squeeze on household spending: electricity bills rose up to 14% this month after municipal surcharges, pushing shoppers toward cheaper food baskets.

mkt:b3.standing: Latin America’s largest exchange, driven by iron ore, oil and Brazilian rates.
mkt:b3.recent: The index sits at the bottom of its 66-day range, down from 178,400 in mid-May. Brazil's dispute with Washington has run through the period — the US revoked the visa of Brazil's ambassador on 4 August, saying it would restore it if Brasília accepted its choice of envoy — and Lula was nominated for a fourth term on 2 August, at 81 by inauguration.

mkt:bmv.standing: Mexico’s benchmark, tightly coupled to US demand and the peso.
mkt:bmv.recent: The index sits near the bottom of its 67-day range, well below its 13 May high of 70,190, and the domestic news flow has been about security and public health rather than earnings: the US put a $25 million bounty on a top Mexican cartel leader on 5 August, and human screwworm cases passed 500. Nothing in the record ties either directly to the move.

mkt:byma.standing: Priced in a currency that has lost most of its value repeatedly, so the index rises even in bad years. Direction over a day means something; the level does not.
mkt:byma.recent: The index sits near 3,001,000 ARS, roughly a tenth above where it started the 64-day window but well below the 3,380,000 high of 22 July, having drifted down through the weeks since that peak. Nothing in the material here explains the reversal.

mkt:tsx.standing: Energy, mining and banks — a commodity index wearing an equity index’s clothes.

mkt:nyse.standing: The largest equity market on earth. Its close sets the tone every other market opens against.
mkt:nyse.recent: The index closed at a 63-day high on Aug 13, up about 4% since the Jun 10 low of 7267. Nothing in the material explains the climb: the period's news is dominated by the Strait of Hormuz standoff, with Trump halting attacks on Iran on Aug 2 and talks with Iran to reopen the strait reported making progress on Aug 4.

mkt:lse.standing: Most FTSE 100 revenue is earned abroad, so a falling pound tends to push the index up.
mkt:lse.recent: The index sits near the top of its range after climbing from the May low, with domestic regulatory decisions the main UK-facing news: Ofwat provisionally cleared £3.4bn in extra water bill rises, and a weakening of the UK's EV sales mandate that could cost drivers £3bn a year. Nothing in the window explains the day's fall.

mkt:xetra.standing: Germany’s industrial and chemical base — Europe’s clearest export barometer.
mkt:xetra.recent: The index touched a series high of 26,390 on Aug 11 before easing 0.2%, up nearly 10% across the window. Commerzbank said on Aug 6 that teaming up with UniCredit could create value, softening Berlin's position that the takeover was a sovereignty threat, and Adidas reported strong growth on the World Cup.

mkt:euronext-paris.standing: Luxury goods and energy dominate — unusually exposed to Chinese consumer demand.
mkt:euronext-paris.recent: The index sits near its 8,726 high of Aug 10 after climbing roughly 9% over the window, and slipped 0.46% on the day. Nothing in the record explains the move: the French news of the period runs to jellyfish shutting 3.2 gigawatts of nuclear capacity at Gravelines, a record-hot June and July, and TotalEnergies buying Shell's European onshore renewables arm.

mkt:euronext-amsterdam.standing: The world’s oldest exchange, now carried largely by ASML.
mkt:euronext-amsterdam.recent: The index reached its highest level of the window on Aug 13, up roughly a tenth over 67 days from its May 13 low. The material here does not explain the climb: the Amsterdam news in the window covers a hack that froze eight CEVA warehouses across Europe and Shell's agreement to sell its European onshore renewables business, neither of which accounts for the trend.

mkt:bme.standing: Spanish banks with heavy Latin American exposure make this a proxy for both regions.
mkt:bme.recent: The index has climbed steadily to 20,210 on Aug 11, its highest of the window, with no single Spanish event behind the run. The period's domestic news was Ceuta, where 72,000 people crossed into a city of 84,000, and the reciprocal border checks that followed Italy's Schengen suspension — neither of which touched the listed banks and utilities.

mkt:borsa-italiana.standing: Banks and utilities, and the market most sensitive to Italian sovereign debt spreads.
mkt:borsa-italiana.recent: The index climbed through a summer of Italian political friction without breaking stride, setting a high of 53,720 on 7 August — the day Spain imposed reciprocal border checks on Italy, a week after Rome suspended Schengen over the 72,000 people who rushed the Ceuta enclave. Milan dealmaking continued regardless: Bending Spoons agreed to buy Airtable for $1.28bn on 4 August.

mkt:six.standing: Nestlé, Roche and Novartis carry the index, which makes it defensive when the world turns risk-off.
mkt:six.recent: The index closed at 14,480, up about 10 percent across the window and near the 14,630 high set on 10 August, well above the 13,210 low of 13 May. Nothing in the available material explains the climb.

mkt:nasdaq-stockholm.standing: Nordic industrials and telecoms, and a useful early read on European capital spending.
mkt:nasdaq-stockholm.recent: The index sits near the top of its range after climbing through the summer, peaking on Aug 5. The one European industrial story in the window is Porsche SE pressing Volkswagen over excess capacity, which does not explain a Stockholm move; the input carries no Swedish or Nordic driver for the run-up.

mkt:tase.standing: Trades Sunday to Thursday. Heavily weighted to banks, defence and technology.

xag.standing: A silver-backed digital token tracking the spot price of an ounce of silver. Silver is both a monetary metal and an industrial input — for solar panels, electronics and brazing alloys — so it moves on investment demand and factory demand at once.
xag.recent: The move follows Washington's polysilicon price floor, which raises the cost of the other core solar-panel input and puts pressure on the metals used alongside it. Silver-backed KAG has climbed from $29.80 on Aug 6 to $64.41 on Aug 14, more than doubling within the month-long window.

wiki-spain.standing: Wikipedia's article on Spain, and how many people read it each day. Attention to a country page rises when that country is the setting for something — a disaster, an election, a border crisis, or an event people travel to see.
wiki-spain.recent: Two Spanish stories ran through the window. Ceuta absorbed 72,000 crossings into a city of 84,000, with 57 bodies recovered, and Italy suspended Schengen over it before Spain imposed reciprocal checks on the Italian border. Then Wednesday's total eclipse crossed Burgos, Zaragoza and Teruel, where totality lasted 81 seconds.

poly-will-there-be-no-change-in-fed-inte.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether the Federal Reserve leaves its policy rate unchanged at the next meeting. It prices what traders will pay for that outcome, so it moves with anything that shifts the central bank's hand — inflation data, labour figures, or pressure on the institution itself.
poly-will-there-be-no-change-in-fed-inte.recent: The contract climbed from 39 on Aug 1 to 73 on Aug 14, with the move building after Trump again sought to fire Fed governor Cook on Aug 7, reviving the fight over Fed independence — a dispute that argues for the Fed holding steady rather than acting under pressure. Polymarket separately overhauled its rules on Aug 7 after a study found fraud.

wiki-turkey.standing: Daily pageviews for the English Wikipedia article on Turkey, a proxy for how many people are looking the country up. Attention series like this spike when a country enters a story most readers only half-know.
wiki-turkey.recent: Turkey signed a collective-defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan at Mecca on 7 August, with defence chiefs and military heads now forming a standing joint command, and Egypt staying out. Ankara also passed a law on PKK disarmament that never names Abdullah Öcalan's release, and rationed Bosphorus passage under Montreux.

poly-will-nigel-farage-win-at-least-80-o.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether Nigel Farage clears an 80% vote share in a British election. Prediction markets price outcomes as tradable odds, so the number is what traders will pay for that result rather than a poll or a forecast.
poly-will-nigel-farage-win-at-least-80-o.recent: Polls opened Thursday in the Clacton by-election, where Farage faces a field the two main British parties declined to contest — including the novelty candidate Count Binface. With the majors standing aside but minor candidates on the ballot, traders cut the odds of an 80% share from 23% to 5% on the same day.

poly-will-marco-rubio-win-the-2028-us-pr.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether Marco Rubio wins the 2028 US presidential election. The price is what traders will pay for that outcome, quoted as a percentage, and it moves as candidates enter, exit or stumble rather than on any poll.
poly-will-marco-rubio-win-the-2028-us-pr.recent: Nothing in the material explains the move. The contract drifted down over the month, from 14% on 15 July to a low of 12% on 27 July, and sits at 13%. The prediction-market news in the window concerns the venues themselves — a federal regulator overriding a state ban on Kalshi in New York, and payout concentration on Polymarket — not the field.

poly-will-venezuela-recognize-israel-by-.standing: A Polymarket contract that pays out if Venezuela formally recognises Israel before the year ends. The price is what traders will pay for that outcome — a bet on Caracas breaking with a long alignment against Israel.
poly-will-venezuela-recognize-israel-by-.recent: Caracas restored consular ties with Israel on 11 August, ending 17 years of severed relations, and the price ran to 56 by 13 August. Consular ties are not recognition, and the market has since given the entire move back, trading at 13.
